## Appendix B Intensity Mapping Instrumental Effects

### B.1 Angular and Radial Window Functions

Just like for the CMB, a line intensity map signal will be convolved by the instrument. Yet while a CMB map is only convolved by the beam in two dimensions, an intensity map will also be convolved along the line-of-sight due to the spectral window in frequency space. In this section, we derive the angular (beam) and radial (spectral) window functions that can be applied to the LIM signal. Throughout this derivation, any integrals over $r$ will be understood to be over the range $r_{\rm min}<r<r_{\rm max}$ .

We start by defining a window function in real space $D(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}|\mathbf{r})$ such that the observed map $T^{\rm obs}(\mathbf{r})$ is a convolution of the true map $T(\mathbf{r})$ with the window function, assuming no instrumental noise or masking, according to

$$ \displaystyle T^{\rm obs}(\mathbf{r})=\int d^{3}r^{\prime}\,D(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}|\mathbf{r})T(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,. $$

Next, we assume that the angular and radial window functions are separable such that $D(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}|\mathbf{r})=A(r^{\prime}|r)B(\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime}|\mathbf{\hat{r}})$ where $A(r^{\prime}|r)$ and $B(\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime}|\mathbf{\hat{r}})$ are the radial and angular window functions, respectively. This allows us to rewrite the convolution as

$$ \displaystyle T^{\rm obs}(\mathbf{r})=\int dr^{\prime}r^{\prime 2}\,A(r^{\prime}|r)\int d\Omega B(\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime}|\mathbf{\hat{r}})T(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,. $$

It can be shown that the SFB moments of the observed map can be written in the form

$$ \displaystyle T_{\ell mn}^{\rm obs} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\tau_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}T_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\int dr\,r^{2}\,dr^{\prime}\,r^{\prime 2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r)A(r^{\prime}|r)j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}r^{\prime}) \displaystyle\times\int d\Omega\,d\Omega^{\prime}\,Y_{\ell m}^{*}(\mathbf{\hat{r}})B(\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime}|\mathbf{\hat{r}})Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime})\,. $$

By taking the covariance of these moments, we find

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle T_{\ell_{1}m_{1}n_{1}}^{\rm obs}T_{\ell_{2}m_{2}n_{2}}^{\rm obs,*}\right\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n_{1}^{\prime}n_{2}^{\prime}}\tau_{\ell^{\prime}n_{1}^{\prime}}\tau_{\ell^{\prime}n_{2}^{\prime}}C_{\ell^{\prime}n_{1}^{\prime}n_{2}^{\prime}}\int dr_{1}\,r_{1}^{2}\,dr_{2}\,r_{2}^{2}j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k_{\ell^{\prime}n_{1}^{\prime}}r_{1})j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k_{\ell^{\prime}n_{2}^{\prime}}r_{2})j_{\ell_{1}}(k_{\ell_{1}n_{1}}r_{1})j_{\ell_{2}}(k_{\ell_{2}n_{2}}r_{2}) \displaystyle\times\int d\Omega_{1}\,d\Omega_{2}\,Y_{\ell_{1}m_{1}}^{*}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{1})Y_{\ell_{2}m_{2}}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{2})Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}^{*}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{1})Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{2})W_{\ell^{\prime}n_{1}^{\prime}n_{2}^{\prime}}^{A}(r_{1},r_{2})W^{B}_{\ell^{\prime}}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{1},\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{2})\,, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle W_{\ell nn^{\prime}}^{A}(r_{1},r_{2}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\frac{\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n_{1}}r)A(r|r_{1})}{j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n_{1}}r_{1})}\right) \displaystyle\times\left(\frac{\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n_{2}}r)A(r|r_{2})}{j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n_{2}}r_{2})}\right)\,, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle W_{\ell}^{B}(r_{1},r_{2})=\frac{1}{P_{\ell}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{2})}\int d\Omega\,d\Omega^{\prime}P(\mathbf{\hat{r}}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime})B(\mathbf{\hat{r}}|\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{1})B(\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime}|\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{2})\,. $$

A simpler expression for the mode covariance arises if it is assumed that $A(r^{\prime}|r)$ and $B(\mathbf{\hat{r}}^{\prime}|\mathbf{\hat{r}})$ are both highly peaked, in which case $W_{\ell nn^{\prime}}^{A}$ and $W_{\ell}^{B}$ should be independent of pixel locations $\mathbf{r}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{r}_{2}$ . In this case, the integrals in Eq. 132 can be performed, giving us

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle T_{\ell_{1}m_{1}n_{1}}^{\rm obs}T_{\ell_{2}m_{2}n_{2}}^{\rm obs,*}\right\rangle=W_{\ell_{1}n_{1}n_{2}}^{A}W_{\ell_{1}}^{B}C_{\ell_{1}n_{1}n_{2}}\delta_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}\delta_{m_{1}m_{2}} $$

For the analytical formulae, this representation for the radial and angular harmonic window functions will be retained. In Appendix B.2 we derive that the radial harmonic window function can be written as a sinc function in the form

$$ \displaystyle W_{\ell nn^{\prime}}^{A}=A(k_{\ell n})A(k_{\ell n^{\prime}})\,, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A(k)=\frac{\pi}{4}\left[{\rm sinc}\left(\frac{k\Delta r-\pi}{2}\right)+{\rm sinc}\left(\frac{k\Delta r+\pi}{2}\right)\right]\,. $$

where $\Delta r$ is the full width of the radial window.

### B.2 Spectral Window Function

Here we derive the radial harmonic window function $W_{\ell nn^{\prime}}^{A}=A_{\ell}(k_{\ell n})A_{\ell}(k_{\ell n^{\prime}})$ , where

$$ \displaystyle A_{\ell}(k)=\frac{\int dr^{\prime}r^{\prime 2}A(r^{\prime}|r)j_{\ell}(kr^{\prime})}{j_{\ell}(kr)}\,, $$

and $A(r^{\prime}|r)$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle A(r^{\prime}|r)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{\pi}{2\Delta r\,r^{\prime 2}}\cos\left[\frac{\pi(r^{\prime}-r)}{\Delta r}\right]&r-\Delta r/2<r^{\prime}<r+\Delta r/2\\
0&{\rm otherwise}\end{array}\right.\,, $$

where $\Delta r$ is the full width of the radial window. This is similar to the window assumed in L17, except we add an extra pre-factor to make it normalize conveniently. Technically the integration over $r$ should be over the range $r_{\rm min}<r<r_{\rm max}$ ; however, since the window function A(r’|r) is expected to be relatively narrow, we can extend the integration range to $r>0$ without losing accuracy. We are mainly going to consider the case where the modes are more radial than angular, $\ell\ll kr$ . However, for the case where $\ell\gtrsim kr$ , $j_{\ell}(kr)$ is a smooth, monotonic function that can be taken out of the integral compared to the highly-peaked $A(r^{\prime}|r)$ , which itself is normalized. Thus, for $\ell\gtrsim kr$ , $A_{\ell}(k)\simeq 1$ .

For $\ell\ll kr$ , we can use the approximation

$$ \displaystyle j_{\ell}(x)=\frac{1}{x}\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi\ell}{2}\right)\,, $$

allowing us to write the numerator of Eq. 138, which we label $Q$ , as

$$ \displaystyle Q=\frac{1}{k}\int_{0}^{\infty}dr^{\prime}\,r^{\prime}\sin\left(kr^{\prime}-\frac{\pi\ell}{2}\right)A(r^{\prime}|r)\,. $$

Since $A(r^{\prime}|r)$ is cut off for $r^{\prime}>r+\Delta r/2$ , it is fine to extend the integral out to infinity. We evaluate this integral using a similar trick as was performed in L17. First, we convert the sine function to an exponential with a derivative.

$$ \displaystyle Q=-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\left\{{\rm Re}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}dr^{\prime}\,e^{-i\alpha kr^{\prime}+i\pi\ell/2}A(r^{\prime}|r)\right]\right\}_{\alpha=1}\,. $$

Then, we define a new function $C(r^{\prime})=A(r^{\prime}+r|r)$ which can be written as

$$ \displaystyle C(r^{\prime}|r)\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{\pi}{2\Delta r\,(r+r^{\prime})^{2}}\cos\left[\frac{\pi r}{\Delta r}\right]&-\Delta r/2<r^{\prime}<+\Delta r/2\\
0&{\rm otherwise}\end{array}\right. $$

Given this, we find

$$ \displaystyle Q \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\left\{{\rm Re}\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,e^{-i\alpha kx}e^{-i\alpha kr+i\pi\ell/2}C(x)\right]\right\}_{\alpha=1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\left\{{\rm Re}\left[e^{-i\alpha kr+i\pi\ell/2}\tilde{C}(\alpha k)\right]\right\}_{\alpha=1}\,, $$

where we define $x\equiv r^{\prime}-r$ and we can extend the integral out to $-\infty$ since $C(x<-\Delta r/2)=0$ , allowing to then define the Fourier transform $\tilde{C}(k)$ . Next, we make the argument that $C(x)$ is approximately an even function in the limit where $r^{\prime}\ll r$ . Under this approximation, we can apply the Re operator to just the exponential, giving us

$$ \displaystyle Q \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{k^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha}\left[\cos\left(\alpha kr-\frac{\pi\ell}{2}\right)\tilde{C}(\alpha k)\right]_{\alpha=1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{k}\left[r\sin\left(kr-\frac{\pi\ell}{2}\right)\tilde{C}(k)-\cos\left(kr-\frac{\pi\ell}{2}\right)\frac{\partial\tilde{C}}{\partial k}\right]\,. $$

Inserting this into Eq. 138, we can write

$$ \displaystyle A_{\ell}(k)=r^{2}\tilde{C}(k)-r\cot\left(kr-\frac{\pi\ell}{2}\right)\frac{\partial\tilde{C}}{\partial k}\,. $$

Now we evaluate $\tilde{C}(k)$ . Using the $r^{\prime}<<r$ approximation, which allows us to just evaluate the real part of the Fourier transform, we find

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{C}(k) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\pi}{2\Delta r\,r^{2}}\int_{-\Delta r/2}^{\Delta r/2}dr\cos(kr)\cos\left(\frac{\pi r}{\Delta r}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\pi}{4r^{2}}\left[{\rm sinc}\left(\frac{k\Delta r-\pi}{2}\right)+{\rm sinc}\left(\frac{k\Delta r+\pi}{2}\right)\right]\,. $$

From this, we know $\partial\tilde{C}/\partial k\propto\Delta r/r\ll 1$ such that we can approximate $A_{\ell}(k)\simeq r^{2}\tilde{C}(k)$ , which gives us Eq. 137.

### B.3 Instrumental Noise

Here we derive the instrumental noise contribution to the covariance of the SFB moments. In this analysis we will set each three-dimensional pixel, or voxel, to be labeled by an index such that the noise fluctuations are labeled $T_{i}^{N}$ . We assume that the noise fluctuations are uncorrelated between voxels and that their distribution varies only with frequency, and thus the radial coordinate for a given line. This gives us a noise covariance matrix $\left\langle T_{i}^{N}T_{j}^{N}\right\rangle=\sigma_{N,i}^{2}\delta_{ij}$ .

We begin by writing the SFB moment for the noise fluctuations as a sum over voxels

$$ \displaystyle T_{\ell mn}^{N}=\sum_{i}\Delta_{i}Y_{\ell m}^{*}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{i})j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r_{i})T_{i}^{N}\,, $$

where $\Delta_{i}$ is the volume of voxel $i$ , given by $\Delta_{i}=\Delta\Omega\Delta r_{i}r_{i}^{2}$ . Taking the covariance, we find

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle T_{\ell mn}^{N}T_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}^{N}\right\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i}\Delta_{i}^{2}Y_{\ell m}^{*}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{i})Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\mathbf{\hat{r}}_{i}) \displaystyle\times j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r_{i})j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}r_{i})\sigma_{N,i}^{2}\,. $$

Converting back from a sum to an integral, we can write the covariance, after integrating over angle, as

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle T_{\ell mn}^{N}T_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}^{N}\right\rangle=N_{\ell nn^{\prime}}\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{mm^{\prime}}\,, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle N_{\ell nn^{\prime}}=\int_{r_{\rm min}}^{r_{\rm max}}dr\,r^{2}\Delta(r)j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r)j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n^{\prime}}r)\sigma_{N}^{2}(r)\,, $$

and $\Delta(r)$ is the size of the voxel as a function or $r$ . The voxel depth is determined by the frequency bin size, such that we can write

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(r)=\Delta\Omega\Delta\nu\left|\frac{dr}{d\nu}\right|r^{2}\,, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{dr}{d\nu}\right|=\frac{c[1+z(r)]}{\nu H[z(r)]}\,. $$

Using the results from the previous section, we can now write

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle T_{\ell_{1}m_{1}n_{1}}^{\rm obs}T_{\ell_{2}m_{2}n_{2}}^{\rm obs,*}\right\rangle=\left[W_{\ell_{1}n_{1}n_{2}}^{AB}C_{\ell_{1}n_{1}n_{2}}+N_{\ell_{1}n_{1}n_{2}}\right]\delta_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}\delta_{m_{1}m_{2}}\,, $$

where we define $W_{\ell n_{1}n_{2}}^{AB}\equiv W_{\ell n_{1}n_{2}}^{A}W_{\ell}^{B}$ .

## Appendix C Proof of Form of Quadratic Estimator

Here we prove that our lensing estimator is the most general quadratic estimator that can be constructed for this problem. Consider a general quadratic estimator for $\phi(\hat{n})$

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\phi}(\hat{n}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int d^{3}xd^{3}y\widetilde{T}(\vec{x})\widetilde{T}(\vec{y})G(\vec{x},\vec{y},\hat{n}). $$

We may expand $\hat{\phi}$ and $\widetilde{T}$ in spherical harmonics and SFB series respectively to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\phi}_{LM} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\sum_{mm^{\prime}}\sum_{nn^{\prime}}\widetilde{T}_{\ell mn}\widetilde{T}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\tau_{\ell n}\tau_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int d^{3}xd^{3}yd\hat{n}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}x)j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}y) \displaystyle\times Y^{*}_{LM}(\hat{n})Y_{\ell m}(\hat{x})Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\hat{y})G(\vec{x},\vec{y},\hat{n}). $$

Now, $G(\vec{x},\vec{y},\hat{n})$ depends on three directions, thus it may be expanded in tripolar spherical harmonics as

$$ \displaystyle G(\vec{x},\vec{y},\hat{n}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}L^{\prime}}\sum_{m_{1}m_{2}M^{\prime}}g_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}L^{\prime}}^{mm^{\prime}M}(x,y)\left({\begin{array}[]{ccc}\ell_{1}&\ell_{2}&L^{\prime}\\
m_{1}&m_{2}&M^{\prime}\\
\end{array}}\right) \displaystyle\times Y_{\ell_{1}m_{1}}(\hat{x})Y_{\ell_{2}m_{2}}(\hat{y})Y_{L^{\prime}M^{\prime}}(\hat{n}). $$

One may integrate the angular part of Eq. 160 by using the orthogonality relations of spherical harmonics to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\phi}_{LM} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\sum_{mm^{\prime}}\sum_{nn^{\prime}}(-1)^{\ell+\ell^{\prime}+L+M}\tau_{\ell n}\tau_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\widetilde{T}_{\ell mn}\widetilde{T}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\left({\begin{array}[]{ccc}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\
m&m^{\prime}&-M\\
\end{array}}\right)\int dxdyx^{2}y^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}x)j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}y) \displaystyle\times g_{\ell\ell^{\prime}L}^{mm^{\prime}M}(x,y). $$

Now, one may make the re-definition,

$$ \displaystyle g_{\ell\ell^{\prime}L}^{mm^{\prime}M,nn^{\prime}} \displaystyle\equiv \displaystyle(-1)^{\ell+\ell^{\prime}+L}\tau_{\ell n}\tau_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\int dxdyx^{2}y^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}x) \displaystyle\times j_{\ell^{\prime}}(k_{\ell^{\prime}n^{\prime}}y)g_{\ell\ell^{\prime}L}(x,y)\,, $$

which leaves the estimator in the form

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\phi}_{LM} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell mn}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}(-1)^{M}\left({\begin{array}[]{ccc}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\
m&m^{\prime}&-M\\
\end{array}}\right) \displaystyle\times g_{\ell\ell^{\prime}L}^{mm^{\prime}M,nn^{\prime}}\widetilde{T}_{\ell mn}\widetilde{T}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}. $$

But, $g_{\ell\ell^{\prime}L}^{mm^{\prime}M,nn^{\prime}}$ is to be determined by minimizing $\langle\hat{\phi}_{LM}\hat{\phi}^{*}_{L^{\prime}M^{\prime}}\rangle$ which we assume to be diagonal, i.e., $\propto\delta_{LL^{\prime}}\delta_{MM^{\prime}}$ . This can only be achieved due to the orthogonality of the 3j-symbol, so $g$ cannot depend on $\{m,m^{\prime},M\}$ . So we now have

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\phi}_{LM} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell mn}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}(-1)^{M}\left({\begin{array}[]{ccc}\ell&\ell^{\prime}&L\\
m&m^{\prime}&-M\\
\end{array}}\right) \displaystyle\times g_{\ell\ell^{\prime}L}^{nn^{\prime}}\widetilde{T}_{\ell mn}\widetilde{T}_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}n^{\prime}}. $$

Finally, since we need an unbiased estimator, we need a suitable normalization which we denote as $A_{L}$ . Thus we have the final form of the estimator as given in the main text.

## Appendix D Approximation for Spherical Bessel Function at large $\ell$

Recall an integral representation of $j_{\ell}(x)$

$$ \displaystyle j_{\ell}(x) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x/2)^{\ell}}{\ell!}\int_{-1}^{1}dt\,e^{ixt}(1-t^{2})^{\ell}. $$

It is known that performing a saddle-point approximation (along with a suitable substitution) produces the following approximation for $j_{\ell}(x)$ for the region $x\leq\ell$ ( $\ell\gg 1$ )

$$ \displaystyle j_{\ell}(x) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{e^{\sqrt{\ell^{2}-x^{2}}}}{2x}\left(\frac{\ell-\sqrt{\ell^{2}-x^{2}}}{x}\right)^{\ell}\left(\frac{\ell-\sqrt{\ell^{2}-x^{2}}}{\sqrt{\ell^{2}-x^{2}}}\right)^{1/2}. $$

Similarly, one may use an integral representation for the spherical Hankel function $h_{\ell}^{(1)}(x)$ to saddle-point approximate it in the region $x\geq\ell$ ( $\ell\gg 1$ )

$$ \displaystyle h^{(1)}_{\ell}(x) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{e^{i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}}{x}\left(\frac{\ell-i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}{x}\right)^{\ell}\left(\frac{\ell-i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}{i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}\right)^{1/2}\,, $$

where the real part of this expression gives the approximation for $j_{\ell}(x)$ . We may consider the regime $kr\geq\ell$ in particular with $x\equiv kr$ . Firstly, note,

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\ell-i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}{i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle i\left(1+i\frac{\ell}{2x}+\frac{\ell^{3}}{4x^{3}}+O(\ell^{5}/x^{5}))\right) \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle i. $$

Now we may define $k_{||}^{2}=k^{2}-\ell^{2}/r_{1}^{2}=k^{2}-k_{\perp}^{2}$ . So we have

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sqrt{k_{||}^{2}r^{2}-\ell^{2}(1-r^{2}/r_{1}^{2})} \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\sqrt{k_{||}^{2}r^{2}-\ell^{2}(1-a^{2})} \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle k_{||}r\,, $$

since $a^{2}=1+\frac{1}{N^{2}}$ where $N=\frac{R}{\Delta R}>>1$ . In light of this, we have the following,

$$ \displaystyle e^{i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}} \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle e^{ik_{||}r}\,, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\ell-i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}{x}\right)^{\ell} \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle\left(\frac{\ell-ik_{||}r}{kr}\right)^{\ell} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(\frac{k_{\perp}-ik_{||}}{k}+O((k_{\perp}/k)(1/N))\right)^{\ell}. $$

The correction term above is small since $k_{\perp}/k<1$ and $N>>1$ , so we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\ell-i\sqrt{x^{2}-\ell^{2}}}{x}\right)^{\ell} \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle\left(\frac{k_{\perp}-ik_{||}}{k}\right)^{\ell}. $$

In the $k_{\perp}-k_{||}$ plane we may now make the following redefinition $k_{\perp}+ik_{||}=ike^{-i\varphi_{k}}$ . This makes the above expression simply $e^{i\varphi_{k}\ell-\frac{\pi\ell}{2}}$ . Thus, the final expression for the Bessel function becomes

$$ \displaystyle j_{\ell}(kr) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\sin{(k_{||}r+\varphi_{k}\ell-\pi\ell/2)}}{kr}. $$

Note that in the limit $kr>>\ell\,(k_{||}>>k_{\perp})$ , $\varphi_{k}\approx 0$ and $k\approx k_{||}$ , which recovers the well known approximation for the Bessel function in this regime.

## Appendix E Foregrounds

Foreground contamination in the flat-sky case is rather straightforward, owing to the fact that the foreground power spectrum has a simple expression (L17) which can be derived straightforwardly for a $T(\vec{r})=T(\mathbf{\hat{r}})$ given so,

$$ \displaystyle C_{\ell}^{\text{fg}}(k_{||}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle C^{\text{fg}}_{\ell}\sinc^{2}{(k_{||}\Delta R/2)}\,, $$

for a survey at mean comoving radius $R$ and survey width $\Delta R$ , particularly for a tophat window function (which is the case we are concerning ourselves with in the SFB formalism). In particular, this expression is independent of $k_{\perp}$ since $C^{\text{fg}}_{\ell}$ is actually constant, i.e., one only needs to impose a cutoff $k_{||,\text{min}}$ . Below, we will derive an expression to determine the appropriate methods for foreground cutoffs for SFB, which has a nontrivial expression for foreground power. For instance, it was shown in L17 that the foreground cuts for SFB will be scale-dependent (which is not the case for Plane-Parallel). Here, we will show that the correct cuts in SFB coordinates are given in terms of $k_{||,\rm min}$ by $k^{2}_{\rm min}=k_{||,\rm min}^{2}+\ell^{2}/r_{\rm max}^{2}$ . Note that any radial integrals will be considered to be from $r_{\rm min}$ to $r_{\rm max}$ , but we will not explicitly write the limits.

To start, consider the foreground signal in SFB (L17),

$$ \displaystyle\tau_{\ell n}C_{\ell n}^{\text{fg}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle C_{\ell}^{\text{fg}}\frac{\left[\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r)\right]^{2}}{\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}^{2}(k_{\ell n}r)}\,, $$

In particular, $\tau_{\ell n}C_{\ell n}^{\text{fg}}$ is some nontrivial function which is expected to produce a nontrivial $k_{\ell n,\text{min}}$ corresponding to the plane-parallel $k_{||,\text{min}}$

In particular we wish to examine $\tau_{\ell n}C_{\ell n}^{\text{fg}}$ in the regime $\ell>>1$ and $k_{\ell n}r\gtrsim\ell$ in order to obtain the correct $k_{\text{min}}$ . Using the approximation for $j_{\ell}(kr)$ obtained in Appendix D we have

$$ \displaystyle k_{\ell n}\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\sin{(k_{||,\ell n}r_{\rm max}+\zeta)}-\sin{(k_{||,\ell n}r_{\rm min}+\zeta)}}{k_{||,\ell n}^{2}}+\frac{r_{\rm min}\cos{(k_{||,\ell n}r_{\rm min}+\zeta)}-r_{\rm max}\cos{(k_{||,\ell n}r_{\rm max}+\zeta)}}{k_{||,\ell n}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle R\Delta R\sinc{(k_{||,\ell n}\Delta R/2)}\sin{(k_{||,\ell n}R+\zeta)}+\frac{\Delta R}{k_{||,\ell n}}\sinc{(k_{||,\ell n}\Delta R/2)}\cos{(k_{||,\ell n}R+\zeta)} \displaystyle-\frac{\Delta R}{k_{||,\ell n}}\cos{(k_{||,\ell n}\Delta R/2)}\cos{(k_{||,\ell n}R+\zeta)}\,, $$

where $k_{||,\ell n}^{2}\equiv k_{\ell n}^{2}-\ell^{2}/r_{\rm max}^{2}$ and $\zeta=\varphi_{k}\ell-\pi\ell/2$ . Now since we have $k_{\ell n}r\approx\ell$ , we have $k_{||,\ell n}\approx 0$ (to order 1/N). Thus, $\varphi_{k}\approx\pi/2$ so $\zeta\approx 0$ . So we have

$$ \displaystyle k_{\ell n}\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r) \displaystyle= \displaystyle R\Delta R\sinc{(k_{||}\Delta R/2)}\sin{(k_{||,\ell n}R)} \displaystyle-R\Delta R\frac{\cos(k_{||}R)}{k_{||,\ell n}R} \displaystyle\times(\cos(k_{||}\Delta R/2)-\sinc(k_{||}\Delta R/2)). $$

However, note that in the limit $k_{||}\rightarrow 0$ , particularly for the case $R\gg\Delta R$ , the second term is subdominant. So to leading order, we may say

$$ \displaystyle k_{\ell n}\int dr\,r^{2}j_{\ell}(k_{\ell n}r) \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle R\Delta R\sinc{(k_{||,\ell n}\Delta R/2)} \displaystyle\times\sin{(k_{||,\ell n}R)}. $$

Next we need the denominator which is just $W_{\ell\ell}(k,k)$ , i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{2k^{2}}{\Delta R}W_{\ell\ell}(k,k) \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle\cos(0)\sinc(0)-\cos(2k_{||}R)\sinc(k_{||}\Delta R) \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle 1\,, $$

since $k_{||}\approx 0$ . To complete, we have

$$ \displaystyle\tau_{\ell n}C_{\ell n}^{\text{fg}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2C_{\ell}R^{2}\Delta R\sinc^{2}(k_{||,\ell n}\Delta R/2)\sin^{2}{(k_{||,\ell n}R)}\,, $$

However, we may average out the oscillatory part of this expression as in L17, which gives exactly that $\tau_{\ell n}C_{\ell n}\approx R^{2}\Delta RC_{\ell}(k_{||,\ell n})$ when $k_{\ell n}R\gtrsim\ell$ . This analysis indicates that the correct contours should be $k_{\text{min}}^{2}=k_{||,\text{min}}^{2}+\frac{\ell^{2}}{r_{\rm max}^{2}}$ , as shown in Fig. 9.
